● A critical moment for higher education
"The humanities are not a counterweight to technology — they are its conscience"
01
Reclaim the Humanities
In STEM environments, humanistic inquiry is too often treated as ornamental. It should be structural. How we understand power, difference, and narrative determines what we build, how, and for whom.
02
Center Lived Experience
Grounded, relational knowledge — rooted in community, place, and history — produces more accountable, verified, and hence more efficient systems than detached, algorithmic thinking. This is not a soft argument. It is an epistemological one.
03
Reimagine Technology, Society, and Law through the Banality of Empathy
Artificial intelligence needs human intelligence. Rationality is balanced by empathy: not as a safety layer added at the end, but as an architecture woven throughout. PromithAI is the prototype of what that could look like in practice.
Biography

Historian of the interconnected world

Elektra Kostopoulou is a Greek-American historian whose teaching and research engage with the Eastern Mediterranean, Southeast Europe, and the Middle East from the perspective of global queries. Through comparative historical analysis, she explores how complex systems evolve, stabilize, and rupture across time — highlighting recurring structural dynamics in migration, empire, law, and global power.

Although her academic journey has unfolded across global contexts — Greece, Turkey, France, the US — it remains deeply rooted in regional histories and lived experience. She is particularly interested in developing alternatives to detached knowledge systems, emphasizing grounded, relational approaches to power, innovation, and storytelling.

Since joining the Department of History at NJIT / Rutgers Newark, she has developed research and teaching initiatives that highlight the urgent need to prioritize humanistic inquiry within the evolving landscape of STEM education and AI-driven technology. Almost ten years in a technical university have sharpened her conviction: the humanities are not peripheral to the age of AI — they are indispensable to it.

Her current work spans questions of self-determination, the global arms trade from the collapse of the Ottoman Empire to the present. In addition, she is interested in technological innovation that is rooted in the fundamental principle that verified human expertise and lived experience must be woven into the architecture of AI systems, not added as an afterthought.

Research

Areas of expertise and inquiry

01
Empire, Autonomy & the Ottoman World
The late Ottoman Empire as a laboratory for federalism, minority governance, and the negotiation of sovereignty — from Crete to the Balkans to the Middle East.
02
Migration, Refugees & Population Exchange
Forced and voluntary population movements across the Eastern Mediterranean, including the 1923 Greco-Turkish exchange, Syrian displacement, and the politics of refugeehood.
03
Marginalized Communities & Self-Determination
The history of the Greek Roma, the politics of identity and recognition, and what minority histories reveal about the limits of nationalist frameworks.
04
Global Arms Trade & Industrial Power
How weapons manufacturing has shaped international conflict from the collapse of the Ottoman Empire through WWI to the contemporary military-industrial complex.
05
Humanities in STEM & AI Literacy
Developing interdisciplinary frameworks that bring historical analysis, ethical reasoning, and lived experience into technical education — and into the design of AI systems.
06
Human-AI Civic Intelligence
Embedding verified human expertise and community knowledge into AI-generated outputs across medicine, education, law, and rights defense.
